section.title: The Crucifixion and Burial
section.sectionRationale: The center of the Gospel: Jesus is crucified between two robbers, mocked as king, and cries out in God-forsaken darkness before yielding up His spirit. The temple veil tears, the earth quakes, a centurion confesses Him Son of God, and He is buried in a sealed, guarded tomb.
section.thesis: On the cross the King of the Jews bears the darkness of God-forsaken judgment for sinners; His death tears open the way to God, moves a pagan soldier to confess Him Son of God, and He is laid in a borrowed tomb, sealed and guarded, awaiting the third day.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the crucifixion and the mockery; the darkness, the cry of dereliction, and the death with its signs; the burial by Joseph of Arimathea; and the sealing of the tomb and the guard.

units.label: The crucifixion
units.note: the King of the Jews, mocked

verses.text: Along the way they found a man from Cyrene, named Simon, and they forced him to carry the cross of Jesus.
And when they came to a place called Golgotha, which means The Place of the Skull,
they offered Him wine to drink, mixed with gall; but after tasting it, He refused to drink it.
When they had crucified Him, they divided up His garments by casting lots.
And sitting down, they kept watch over Him there.
Above His head they posted the written charge against Him: THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS.
Two robbers were crucified with Him, one on His right and the other on His left.
And those who passed by heaped abuse on Him, shaking their heads
and saying, “You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days, save Yourself! If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross!”
In the same way, the chief priests, scribes, and elders mocked Him, saying,
“He saved others, but He cannot save Himself. He is the King of Israel! Let Him come down now from the cross, and we will believe in Him.
He trusts in God. Let God deliver Him now if He wants Him. For He said, ‘I am the Son of God.’”
In the same way, even the robbers who were crucified with Him berated Him.

units.label: The death of Jesus
units.note: darkness, the cry, and the torn veil

verses.text: From the sixth hour until the ninth hour darkness came over all the land.
About the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eli, Eli, lema {{sabachthani|sabachthani}}?” which means, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
When some of those standing there heard this, they said, “He is calling Elijah.”
One of them quickly ran and brought a sponge. He filled it with sour wine, put it on a reed, and held it up for Jesus to drink.
But the others said, “Leave Him alone. Let us see if Elijah comes to save Him.”
When Jesus had cried out again in a loud voice, He yielded up His spirit.
At that moment the {{katapetasma|veil}} of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom. The earth quaked, and the rocks were split.
The tombs broke open, and the bodies of many saints who had fallen asleep were raised.
After Jesus’ resurrection, when they had come out of the tombs, they entered the holy city and appeared to many people.
When the centurion and those with him who were guarding Jesus saw the earthquake and all that had happened, they were terrified and said, “Truly this was the {{huios|Son}} of God.”
And many women were there, watching from a distance. They had followed Jesus from Galilee to minister to Him.
Among them were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of Zebedee’s sons.
When it was evening, there came a rich man from Arimathea named Joseph, who himself was a disciple of Jesus.
He went to Pilate to ask for the body of Jesus, and Pilate ordered that it be given to him.
So Joseph took the body, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth,
and placed it in his own new tomb that he had cut into the rock. Then he rolled a great stone across the entrance to the tomb and went away.
Mary Magdalene and the other Mary were sitting there opposite the tomb.
The next day, the one after Preparation Day, the chief priests and Pharisees assembled before Pilate.
“Sir,” they said, “we remember that while He was alive that deceiver said, ‘After three days I will rise again.’

So give the order that the tomb be secured until the third day. Otherwise, His disciples may come and steal Him away and tell the people He has risen from the dead. And this last deception would be worse than the first.”
“You have a guard,” Pilate said. “Go, make the tomb as secure as you know how.”
So they went and secured the tomb by sealing the stone and posting the guard.

sabachthani.gloss: You have forsaken Me. Part of Jesus' cry, Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani, quoting Psalm 22:1 in Aramaic. In the God-forsaken darkness Jesus bears the judgment due to sinners, yet the psalm He quotes moves from anguish to vindication and praise.

katapetasma.gloss: The curtain or veil that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place in the temple, barring access to God's presence. At Jesus' death it is torn from top to bottom, God's own act, opening the way to God through the crucified Christ, Hebrews 10:19-20.

huios.gloss: Son. The pagan centurion, watching Jesus die, confesses truly this was the Son of God, the very title mocked at the cross; at the moment of apparent defeat a Gentile soldier proclaims the truth the whole Gospel has been unfolding.

basic.context: Simon of Cyrene is forced to carry Jesus' cross to Golgotha, where He is crucified between two robbers under the charge King of the Jews. Passersby, leaders, and even the robbers mock Him, taunting Him to save Himself. From noon darkness covers the land; at three Jesus cries out, My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me, and then yields up His spirit. The temple veil tears, the earth quakes, tombs open, and a centurion confesses, Truly this was the Son of God. Women watch from afar. Joseph of Arimathea buries Him in his new tomb, which the leaders seal and guard.
basic.hermeneutics: This is the heart of the Gospel, told with restraint and saturated with Psalm 22 and Isaiah 53. The mockery, save Yourself, unwittingly states the gospel: He could not save others and Himself. The cry of dereliction and the darkness signal that Jesus bears God's judgment. The torn veil interprets His death: access to God is opened. Read the signs, the veil, quake, and centurion, as God's own commentary.
basic.originalLanguages: In the darkness Jesus cries Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani, You have forsaken Me, bearing judgment for sinners. At His death the katapetasma, the veil, is torn open, and a Gentile confesses Him huios, the Son of God.
basic.typology: Jesus fulfills the suffering of Psalm 22, pierced, mocked, His garments divided, and the servant of Isaiah 53. The torn veil fulfills the whole temple system, opening the way into God's presence. The new tomb and the burial fulfill Isaiah 53's grave with the rich.
basic.christ: Jesus is the King reigning from the cross, the forsaken Son bearing the judgment of God, the true temple whose death opens access to God, and the Son of God confessed by a pagan soldier at the moment He dies.
basic.god: God is at work in the darkness: the Father does not spare His Son but gives Him up for us, and by tearing the veil He opens His own presence to sinners. The signs are His testimony that this death is the turning point of the world.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 22 is quoted and enacted throughout. Isaiah 53 gives the pierced servant buried with the rich. Hebrews 10 explains the torn veil as new access to God. Romans 8 declares God did not spare His own Son.
basic.oneStory: At the cross the whole story bends to its center: the King reigns from a tree, bearing the God-forsaken judgment sinners deserve, and His death tears open the way into God's presence that sin had closed since Eden. A Gentile confesses Him Son of God, a first fruit of the nations. He is buried, sealed, and guarded, and all creation holds its breath for the third day, when the story will turn from death to life.

context.literary:
Matthew tells the crucifixion with great restraint and arranges it in three movements around the cry in verse 46. In verses 32 to 44 the world mocks: soldiers, passers-by, rulers and robbers all speak, and all say some version of 'Save Yourself.' In verse 45 to 50 the sky goes dark, Jesus speaks, and He dies. In verses 51 to 56 God speaks through events. The veil, the earthquake, the split rocks and the opened tombs form a chain with one pattern, and a pagan soldier is the first to read it.

The mockery is structured by three taunts that repeat the temptations of Matthew 4. 'If You are the Son of God,' the devil said in the wilderness, and 'If You are the Son of God, come down from the cross' says the crowd in verse 40. The leaders add 'He trusts in God, let God deliver Him,' verse 43, which is almost word for word what the enemies of the righteous sufferer say in Psalm 22:8. The taunts are meant to tempt Him to prove His sonship by escape, and the Gospel's answer is that He proves it by staying.

Matthew's narration is plain: 'they crucified Him,' verse 35, in a subordinate clause, with no description of the nails. The restraint puts all the weight on what comes around it, the casting of lots, the charge above His head, the darkness, the cry.

The scene is also bracketed by names. A man named Simon, from Cyrene, carries the cross at the start, and women named Mary stand watching at the end and later at the tomb, verses 55, 56 and 61. These are the witnesses who connect the cross, the burial and the empty tomb of chapter 28.

The chapter ends with a guard at the tomb, verses 62 to 66, a section found only in Matthew, whose purpose is to prepare for the resurrection account that follows.
context.historical:
Crucifixion was a Roman punishment reserved for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals, designed to be as public and degrading as possible. Roman citizens were normally spared it. Condemned men were often made to carry the crossbeam to the place of execution, and when a soldier compelled a bystander to carry it, as with Simon of Cyrene, perhaps because the prisoner was weakened by the flogging of verse 26. Mark adds that Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus, Mark 15:21, a detail that suggests the sons were known to the first readers. Cyrene was a city in North Africa with a large Jewish community.

Golgotha is the Aramaic for 'skull,' and the site lay outside the city wall, which fits the Letter to the Hebrews' remark that Jesus 'suffered outside the city gate,' Hebrews 13:12. The offered drink in verse 34 echoes Psalm 69:21, where gall and vinegar are given to the sufferer. The soldiers took the clothing of the condemned as a perquisite, and the placard giving the charge was fixed above the head, so the title 'King of the Jews' was meant as a warning to any other would-be king.

The darkness from the sixth to the ninth hour is from noon to three in the afternoon. The prophets had linked darkness at noon with the Lord's judgment, Amos 8:9, and the plague of darkness in Egypt had been felt as a tangible dread, Exodus 10:21 to 23. The last cry, 'Eli, Eli,' is Hebrew, which is why some hearers thought He was calling for Elijah, a prophet whose return was expected, Malachi 4:5.

The veil of the temple was the heavy curtain with cherubim worked into it that separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, Exodus 26:31 to 33. Joseph of Arimathea's act was a daring one: Deuteronomy 21:23 required the burial of an executed man the same day, and Pilate could grant the request of a person of standing. A tomb cut into rock, sealed by a rolling stone, was typical of a wealthy family. The leaders' request for a guard shows how well they remembered what Jesus had said about the third day.
context.canonical:
Few passages in the Gospels are so thick with Scripture. Psalm 22 stands behind much of the scene: the dividing of the garments by lot, verse 35 and Psalm 22:18; the shaking heads, verse 39 and Psalm 22:7; the mocking 'He trusts in God, let God deliver Him,' verse 43 and Psalm 22:8; and the cry from the opening line, verse 46 and Psalm 22:1. The psalm moves from agony to praise, and its ending proclaims that 'all the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the LORD,' Psalm 22:27.

The vinegar and gall recall Psalm 69:21. Isaiah 53 supplies the other half of the picture: 'numbered with the transgressors,' Isaiah 53:12, fits the robbers on His right and left, and the grave 'with a rich man in His death,' Isaiah 53:9, fits Joseph's tomb. The darkness at noon recalls Amos 8:9, and the earthquake and the opened graves belong with the hope of Ezekiel 37:12 to 14, Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2.

The torn veil is explained by Hebrews. The way into the Most Holy Place 'had not yet been disclosed' while the first tabernacle stood, Hebrews 9:8, but now believers have confidence to enter 'by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:19 and 20.

The New Testament then reads the cross as the center of everything. Paul reminds the Corinthians that 'Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,' 1 Corinthians 15:3, and says that we are redeemed from the curse of the law because Christ became a curse, Galatians 3:13. Luke adds words of Jesus at the cross that Matthew does not record, 'Father, forgive them,' Luke 23:34, and 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit,' Luke 23:46, taken from Psalm 31:5, and John records 'It is finished,' John 19:30.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew wanted his readers to see in Jesus' death the fulfilment of the Scriptures, and not a tragic accident. The details of the scene are chosen because they match what David and Isaiah had written. When the soldiers divide the clothing and the passers-by shake their heads, the reader is meant to hear the psalm underneath.

He wanted to show that Jesus died as the King and Son of God, not in spite of being such but in the very act of dying. The charge posted above His head and the taunts of the crowd both proclaim the truth without understanding it, and the pagan soldier finally says it with understanding. Matthew intends the cross to be the place where Jesus' identity is most fully shown.

He wanted his readers to grasp that this death accomplishes something. The darkness and the cry show that the sufferer is bearing the judgment of God, and the torn veil, the earthquake and the opened graves show that the death has consequences for the whole order of things: access to God is open and the power of death is broken. Matthew places these signs not as decoration but as God's own interpretation of what happened.

He also anchors the story in witnesses. Named women saw it, a respected disciple buried Him, and even the enemies took steps to secure the tomb. The Gospel's confession that He rose depends on the fact that He really died and was really buried.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes the death of Jesus and does not command anyone to repeat it. The mockery and cruelty are not endorsed, and the unrepeatable cry of abandonment is not a pattern for believers to expect, since Jesus stood in a place no one else can stand. Christians are promised that God will never leave them or forsake them, Hebrews 13:5, precisely because Jesus was forsaken.

What does carry forward is clear. Believers are told to look to the cross for the meaning of their own forgiveness: 'Christ died for us,' Romans 5:8. They are told to follow Jesus in non-retaliation, 1 Peter 2:23, and to take up their cross in the sense of being willing to suffer for Him, Matthew 16:24. The detail that Simon was made to carry the cross beam is not an instruction but a picture of that discipleship, since the same words, 'take up the cross,' appear in Jesus' call.

The phenomena at the moment of death are descriptions of what God did. The tearing of the veil does not command the destruction of any building, and the opened tombs do not set a pattern for resurrection events in daily life. They are signs, and they should be read as signs of what the death accomplished.

Joseph and the women are examples of loyal devotion in a hard hour. They do not prescribe particular funeral customs, but they show the faithfulness of ordinary people who stay near Jesus when public opinion has turned.

debates.question: What does Jesus' cry, 'My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?' mean?

views.label: A real abandonment in which He bears judgment
views.case: The darkness, the cry and the title 'My God' rather than 'Father' fit the claim that Jesus was actually bearing the penalty for sin. Paul says God made Him 'to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, and that He became a curse, Galatians 3:13. Calvin and the Reformers read the cry this way, as the experience of the wrath sinners deserve.

views.label: A prayer that quotes Psalm 22, whose whole movement is hope
views.case: Jesus speaks the first line of a psalm that ends in vindication and in the nations turning to the LORD, Psalm 22:24 and 27 to 31. On this view He prays the whole psalm in a single line, identifying with the sufferer whose cry is heard, and the cry expresses suffering and trust together.

views.label: The cry of dereliction is real, but the Trinity is not torn
views.case: Many theologians say the Son truly experienced the loss of the Father's felt presence while the Father and Son remained one in love and purpose. John 10:17 and 18 and Luke 23:46 show that He still trusted the Father and offered Himself freely.

debates.bearing: These views are not mutually exclusive. Most traditions hold that the cry is a real expression of bearing sin's judgment, spoken in the words of Scripture and in the confidence that God hears. What no reading may do is soften the horror or the love of it.

debates.question: What are the raised saints of verses 52 and 53?

views.label: A literal event, a first sign of the resurrection to come
views.case: Matthew states that tombs opened and the bodies of many saints 'were raised' and appeared in the holy city after Jesus' resurrection. Read straightforwardly, God gave a visible foretaste that death's hold was broken, with Jesus as 'the firstfruits,' 1 Corinthians 15:20.

views.label: An apocalyptic symbol of the hope of Israel
views.case: Others read the language as a way of saying that the end-time resurrection promised in Ezekiel 37 and Daniel 12:2 was set in motion by the cross, and treat the vivid detail as prophetic imagery, as with the veil and the earthquake.

views.label: A real event of uncertain nature
views.case: Some hold it was real but a restoration to mortal life, like Lazarus, rather than a glorified resurrection, because Christ is called the first to rise in the full sense, Colossians 1:18.

debates.bearing: The text places their coming out of the tombs after Jesus' resurrection, which keeps Him first. Whatever their nature, the sign points to what His death and rising achieve: the dead belong to Him.

debates.question: What does the centurion mean by 'Son of God'?

views.label: A confession of true divine sonship
views.case: The earthquake and the darkness and the manner of His death led the soldier to say it, and Matthew has just told us Jesus' own claim to be the Son of God, verses 40 and 43. At the climax of the Gospel the words carry their full weight.

views.label: A pagan's reverent admiration, 'a son of a god'
views.case: The Greek does not have the article, and a Roman soldier might have meant that He was a divine man or a righteous one. Luke has the centurion say 'Surely this was a righteous man,' Luke 23:47.

views.label: An unintended truth
views.case: Whatever the soldier understood, Matthew intends the reader to hear the full meaning, as with the placard and the mockery earlier.

debates.bearing: Matthew allows the reader to hear the fullest confession whatever the soldier knew. The remarkable fact is that the first to say it is a Gentile, an outsider, which already points to the nations in Matthew 28:19.

study.originalLanguages:
Matthew's Greek preserves the Hebrew sound of the cry. He writes 'Eli, Eli,' which is Hebrew, and not 'Eloi,' the Aramaic form that Mark records, which is why bystanders could think He was calling for Elijah. The following word is Aramaic, and the combination of the languages shows that Jesus quoted the psalm as it was prayed in the speech of His own people. The Greek gloss that follows uses a verb meaning to leave someone behind in a place of need, the verb the Greek Old Testament also uses for Psalm 22:1.

The verb in verse 50 is also striking. Where English says He 'yielded up His spirit,' the Greek says literally that He 'sent away' or 'let go' the spirit, as though the act were His own. This agrees with John 10:18, 'No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord,' and with Luke 23:46, 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.'

In verse 51 the veil 'was torn,' a divine passive, an action done by God and not by any visible hand, and it is done 'from top to bottom,' from above to below. The same verb describes the splitting of the rocks in the same sentence, as though the stone and the curtain share one tearing. In verse 52 the saints are 'raised,' the same verb that Matthew will use for Jesus in 28:6, and verse 53 uses the noun 'resurrection' for His rising, in the phrase 'after His resurrection,' which keeps the order clear: He is raised first and they follow.

The centurion's confession reads, 'Truly God's Son was this one,' with the word 'God's' first for emphasis. The Greek has no article before 'Son,' which has led to the translations 'a son of God' and 'the Son of God.' Both are possible grammatically, but the speech comes straight after the mockery 'If You are the Son of God,' so the context favours the full title. The tense is 'was,' a statement looking back over the whole life now ended.

The compelled bearer of the cross is 'forced' by a Greek verb that came from the Persian courier system and is the one Jesus used in Matthew 5:41 about going the second mile when a soldier compels you. Simon is made to do what Jesus had told disciples to do willingly, and Matthew uses the very words of Jesus' call, 'take up his cross,' in 16:24, for what Simon does.

The women had 'followed and ministered' to Him, the verb 'to serve' that Matthew used for Peter's mother-in-law in Matthew 8:15, and Joseph 'had become a disciple,' with the verb that Jesus uses in the Great Commission, 'make disciples,' Matthew 28:19. At the end, the leaders call Jesus 'that deceiver,' and the 'guard' that Pilate gives them is a Latin loan word, a Roman detachment.

typology.fulfillment: David's psalm describes a righteous man surrounded by mockers who shake their heads and say 'He trusts in the LORD, let the LORD deliver him,' whose garments are divided by lot and whose hands and feet are pierced. Matthew shows these details one by one at the cross, Psalm 22:7, 8, 16 and 18. The correspondence is much more than the experience of any single person, since the psalm that begins in abandonment ends with the nations turning to the LORD, Psalm 22:27, and the cross is where that outcome begins. The type is limited in that David's sufferings were his own, while Christ's are for others.

The curtain with cherubim worked into it, Exodus 26:31 to 33, marked the barrier between God's presence and the people, and only the high priest passed it once a year. At Jesus' death it is torn from top to bottom, and Hebrews explains that believers can now enter 'by the blood of Jesus,' through 'the curtain of His body,' Hebrews 10:19 and 20. The old arrangement pointed forward to this opening. The pattern is not fully set aside as shadow: the reality it foreshadowed is greater than the thing it pictured, as Hebrews 9 shows.

Isaiah 53:9 says that the servant was assigned a grave with the wicked and with a rich man in His death, although He had done no violence. Joseph of Arimathea, described as a rich man and a disciple, gives Jesus his own new tomb, and the body is wrapped in clean linen. The prophecy is fulfilled in a way no one could have arranged, since Jesus died among criminals but was buried by a rich disciple. The fulfilment also looks forward, because a tomb that was new, with no other body in it, makes the resurrection unmistakable.

typology.type: The sealed stone and the guard
typology.fulfillment: A stone over a pit sealed with the royal signet recalls Daniel in the lions' den, Daniel 6:17, when a king sealed the stone so that nothing could be changed. In Matthew the leaders seal the stone and set a guard so that nothing can be changed in the case of Jesus, and yet it is changed. The parallel is a pattern, not a claim of Matthew's text, but it is a natural one: the stone cannot hold a man whom God will raise, as the lions' mouths could not harm Daniel.

study.christ:
This is the place where Jesus is most clearly revealed as King and Saviour at once. The inscription above His head is the Gospel's plainest statement of who He is, and it is written by His enemies: 'THIS IS JESUS, THE KING OF THE JEWS,' verse 37. The mockers say 'He saved others, but He cannot save Himself,' verse 42, and in saying it they unwittingly state the gospel, since to save others He would not save Himself. He could not do both, and He chose to save them.

He is the Son who is forsaken so that sinners will not be. In the darkness He uses the words of the psalm, and the use of 'My God' puts the weight on the covenant relationship that is being strained. Paul says that for our sake God made the sinless one to be sin, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and Romans 8:32 says that God 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all.' The cry is the point at which that giving up is most keenly felt. Yet He does not stop trusting; Luke records that His last words were a prayer to the Father, Luke 23:46.

He is the true temple. When He dies the veil is torn, and Hebrews says the way into the Most Holy Place has been opened through the curtain of His body, Hebrews 10:19 and 20. The temple leaders had accused Him of threatening the sanctuary, and the taunt in verse 40 repeats it: 'You who are going to destroy the temple and rebuild it in three days.' At the moment of His death the old sanctuary's barrier falls, and the promised rebuilding follows in three days.

He is the Lord of life even in death. The earthquake and the opened tombs show that death cannot keep what belongs to Him. He is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. The saints raised after His resurrection are the first fruit of the harvest.

He is the one whom a Gentile confesses. Before any disciple has risen from despair, a Roman soldier says 'Truly this was the Son of God.' This points to the nations, to whom the same Jesus will send His followers.

A caution keeps the reading honest. The details of the sponge, the reed, the number of hours and the names of the women are real and meaningful, but not every one is a hidden symbol. The reliable links are the ones the Gospel and the New Testament make themselves: the psalm, the servant, the veil, the grave and the confession.
study.god:
The most striking thing the passage shows about God is that He is present in the darkness. The sun is darkened over all the land, and the word of Amos 8:9 and the plague of Exodus 10 stand behind it. The Creator who said 'Let there be light' now allows darkness to cover the death of His Son, and the darkness is part of His testimony as well as of His judgment. In the Bible, darkness at the hour of death tells us that something of cosmic significance is under way.

God is a God who judges sin and bears it. The passage does not separate the justice and love of God. The Father who 'did not spare His own Son,' Romans 8:32, is the Father who 'so loved,' and the Son who is forsaken is the Son who gives Himself. Paul says that God proves His love in this, that Christ died for us while we were still sinners, Romans 5:8. The Trinity is not divided in purpose, though the cry shows the cost: the Father, the Son and the Spirit were united in the work of atonement, Hebrews 9:14.

God is the one who interprets the event. When Jesus dies, God speaks by the torn veil, the shaking of the earth, the opened tombs and the confession of the soldier. In this sense the cross is not only an act of man but a word of God. He does not leave the death unexplained. The same God who spoke by the prophets in advance now speaks by signs in the moment, and He will speak again on the third day.

God is faithful to His word of old. The psalm, the servant, the darkness and the grave were all promised, and Matthew presents them as fulfilled. He guards what He has said, even when what He has said involves the suffering of His Son.

God is holy, and the veil shows that holiness is no barrier for those whom the blood has cleansed. For centuries the curtain taught that sinners could not simply walk into His presence. Now He Himself tears it, from top to bottom, and no human hand does so. The same holy God opens the way.

For worship, the cross calls us to silence before the cost of our forgiveness, to gratitude for the access we have, and to confidence that no darkness we pass through is outside His care. The God who answered the cry of the forsaken Son with resurrection is the God who hears ours.

crossReferences.note: The cry of Matthew 27:46 is the first line of David's psalm, 'My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?' Jesus chooses words from Scripture to express the deepest agony, and the psalm that begins in dereliction ends in the praise of the nations. The link shows both the depth of the suffering and the hope that follows.

All who see the sufferer mock, shake their heads and say that he trusts in the LORD, so let the LORD deliver him. The passers-by of Matthew 27:39 and the leaders of verse 43 speak the psalm's taunt almost verbatim, unwittingly confirming that the one they mock is the sufferer the psalm describes.

The psalmist's garments are divided and lots are cast for his clothing. Matthew 27:35 records the soldiers doing exactly this beneath the cross. It is one of the clearest cases in which a detail of the passion was foretold in a psalm centuries earlier.

The servant is assigned a grave with the wicked and with a rich man in His death. Jesus is crucified among robbers, and is then laid by Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, in his own tomb. The two halves of the verse are both fulfilled in the same few hours.

The Lord declares that He will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in the daytime. The darkness of Matthew 27:45 from the sixth hour fits this prophecy, which treats such darkness as a sign of judgment and mourning. The cross is a day of God's reckoning.

Believers have confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, through the curtain of His body. This is the inspired explanation of the torn veil, showing that what happened in the temple was a picture of what was done in Jesus' flesh.

God did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all. The verse is the Father's side of the cross, which the cry of Matthew 27:46 shows from the Son's side. It also draws out the consequence: if God gave the greatest gift, He will not withhold the lesser ones.

Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, quoting Deuteronomy 21:23 about one who hangs on a tree. The cross is the place where the curse is borne, and the urgency of burying Jesus before nightfall in Matthew 27:57 to 60 reflects the same law.

A stone is laid over the mouth of a den and sealed with the king's signet so that nothing concerning Daniel can be changed. Matthew 27:66 describes the leaders sealing the stone and posting a guard. The parallel shows both the attempt to keep the matter closed and the God who delivered Daniel.

Luke records the last words of Jesus as 'Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit,' from Psalm 31:5. Set beside Matthew's cry, they show a Saviour who goes into the darkness and yet places Himself in the Father's hands. The two Gospels together give the full shape of His dying.

study.oneStory:
From the early chapters of Genesis the story has been waiting for this hour. God had said that the day Adam ate he would surely die, Genesis 2:17, and the Bible's whole account of sin is that death passes to all, Romans 5:12. Here the death sentence is borne by one who did not deserve it. The tree in Eden brought a curse on all; the tree at Golgotha takes it away, Galatians 3:13. The man who was told he would return to dust is answered by the one who goes into the dust and is not abandoned there.

The cross also gathers Israel's story. The sanctuary was the place where a holy God lived among sinful people at a distance, with veil and altar and priest. All of that was a pointer. At the death of Jesus the veil comes down and the true sacrifice is made, so that sacrificial worship has found its goal. The Passover lamb, the Day of Atonement, the suffering of the righteous in the psalms and the servant of Isaiah all converge on one place.

It is the centre of the promise to the nations. God had said to Abraham that all peoples on earth would be blessed through him, Genesis 12:3, and the psalm that opens in dereliction ends with the nations bowing before the Lord, Psalm 22:27. The first to confess Jesus at the cross is a Gentile soldier, the first to bury Him with honour is a rich man who had followed in secret, and the first to stay near are the women. The people who gather at the cross are already a sample of the new people of God.

It leads straight to the resurrection. The guard and the seal in verses 62 to 66 are the tomb's last secure moment, and chapter 28 follows with the stone rolled away. The earthquake and the raised saints already announce the end of death's rule, and Paul says that Christ is 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20.

And it ends in the new creation. The Lamb who was slain is worthy to open the scroll and has purchased people from every tribe and language by His blood, Revelation 5:9. There is no temple in the final city, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22, and the veil has no place there. The One who cried out in the darkness will be the light of that city, and 'there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4.

quiz.q: What did the mockers unwittingly reveal when they said He saved others but cannot save Himself?

options.text: The truth of the gospel: to save others, He would not save Himself.
options.note: Their taunt states the very logic of the atonement, that He stayed on the cross to save sinners.

options.text: That Jesus had lost all His power on the cross.
options.note: He could have come down but chose not to; the irony is that His staying is His saving power, not weakness.

options.text: That Jesus had never really helped anyone.
options.note: They admit He saved others; the point is He would not spare Himself in order to save them.

options.text: That Jesus deserved to be on the cross.
options.note: He was innocent; the taunt ironically declares His saving purpose, not His guilt.

quiz.q: What is the significance of the temple veil tearing at Jesus' death?

options.text: God Himself opened the way into His presence through the death of His Son.
options.note: Torn from top to bottom, it signals new access to God, Hebrews 10:19-20.

options.text: The temple was damaged by the earthquake.
options.note: The quake accompanies it, but the tearing of the veil is a purposeful sign of opened access, not mere damage.

options.text: The temple was now to be abandoned by worshipers.
options.note: The point is opened access to God through Christ, not simply abandoning the building.
Matthew presents it as a weighty, God-given sign at the moment of Jesus' death.

quiz.q: Who confessed Jesus as the Son of God at His death, and why is it striking?

options.text: A pagan centurion, using the very title that had been mocked, moved by how Jesus died and the signs.
options.note: Verse 54 shows a Gentile soldier confessing the truth at the cross.

options.text: One of the Jewish leaders who had condemned Him.
options.note: It was a Gentile centurion, not a leader; that a pagan confessed Him is the striking point.

options.text: One of the robbers crucified beside Him.
options.note: In Matthew both robbers berated Him; the confession came from the centurion.

options.text: The crowd that had called for His crucifixion.
options.note: The crowd mocked; it was the centurion who confessed Him Son of God.

quiz.q: Why did the leaders ask Pilate to secure the tomb?

options.text: They remembered Jesus' promise to rise and wanted to prevent any claim of resurrection.
options.note: Verses 63-64 show they sealed and guarded the tomb against His rising, ironically strengthening the evidence.

options.text: They wanted to honor Jesus' body with proper protection.
options.note: Their concern was to prevent a resurrection claim, not to honor Him, which this misreads.

options.text: They feared the disciples would attack them.
options.note: Their stated fear was a stolen-body resurrection claim, not personal attack.

options.text: They believed Jesus would certainly rise again.
options.note: They called it a deception; they sought to prevent, not confirm, a resurrection.

questions: Jesus refused to come down from the cross so that He could save others. How does it change your view of His love to know He stayed there for you?
In the darkness Jesus was forsaken so that His people never will be. When you feel abandoned, how does His cry of dereliction speak to your own?
The veil was torn from top to bottom, opening the way to God. Are you living as someone with free access to God through Christ, or still standing at a distance?
A pagan soldier confessed Jesus as the Son of God by watching how He died. What about the cross most moves you to confess Him as Lord?
The tomb was sealed and guarded, humanly secure against any hope. Where do you need to trust God with a situation that looks sealed shut?

translationNotes.note: Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani is Aramaic (with a Hebrew form of the divine name), quoting Psalm 22:1; the bystanders' confusion with Elijah reflects the similar sound of Eli and Elijah.
The dividing of Jesus' garments by casting lots fulfills Psalm 22:18; some manuscripts add an explicit fulfillment citation, which the BSB places in a footnote.
Matthew alone records the opening of the tombs and the raising of many saints, who appear after Jesus' own resurrection; it is a sign that His death breaks the power of death for His people.
